children: This article has been updated to correct the date of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite's most recent record closing highs. By Joseph Adinolfi
All 11 S&P 500 sectors finished more than 1% lower this week for the first time since April 2025
It was a bad week for stocks on Wall Street.

U.S. stocks have been wobbling for a while, but it really felt like the wheels came off the artificial-intelligence trade this week, as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite erased its year-to-date gains and fell more than 10% in its worst week since March 2020.

When the closing bell rang Friday, the S&P 500 SPX and Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA joined the Nasdaq COMP and the Russell 2000 small-cap index RUT in correction territory. For the S&P 500, it was the first time since the April 2025 tariff tantrum that the index had fallen by 10% or more from a recent closing high - the widely accepted definition of a correction - according to Dow Jones Market Data. The large-cap index also finished below the 7,000 level for the first time since April.

It was just the latest bump in what has been a rough stretch for stocks in the fourth quarter. Major indexes have been struggling since the S&P 500 and Nasdaq tallied their most recent record closing highs on Oct. 6. Back then, the Nasdaq was sitting on a gain of roughly 25% for 2026. As of Friday's close, all of those gains had been wiped out. The index finished in the red for the year for the first time since April.

Shares of Anthropic (ANT) plunged nearly 10% on Friday in the stock's first full day of trading following its market debut, the biggest initial public offering in U.S. history. Shares finished below $90, not far from the offering price of $83.

In a post on X, Dan Ives, a noted tech analyst and partner at merchant bank Yorkville Ives, blamed the selloff on a perfect storm of factors. The Anthropic offering had siphoned money away from other artificial-intelligence-linked investments, he said, while a strengthening U.S. dollar DXY was causing financial conditions to tighten, drawing liquidity out of the market.

Worries about persistent inflation and a Federal Reserve seemingly bent on raising interest rates were inspiring worries of a policy mistake, Ives added. And Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections - not just in Congress, but in several key governor's races - have raised concerns that a more heavy-handed approach to regulation could slow the data-center buildout.
To top it all off, Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA) has raised uncomfortable questions about the financing behind the AI buildout.

"It really is a perfect storm," said Peter Berezin, chief economist at BCA Research, in a conversation with MarketWatch. "We're definitely seeing cracks in the AI narrative, and those cracks are worrying investors."
Nvidia shares have fallen by nearly 50% from their Oct. 6 record high. On Friday, they plunged by double digits, tallying their worst one-day loss since the DeepSeek selloff.

All 11 S&P 500 sectors fell by more than 1% this week for the first time since April 4, 2025 - the week of President Trump's "liberation day" tariff rollout. That caused a gauge that tracks correlation within the index to surge - another sign that the negative sentiment has started to broaden beyond just the AI trade.
"In my career, I can't recall sentiment and fundamentals this far apart," said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at the Founder 100 exchange-traded fund.
2018 redux
The fourth quarter is usually a happy time for investors. It has been the quarter with the strongest average return for the S&P 500 going back to World War II, Dow Jones Market Data showed.

As of Friday, the S&P 500 was on track to buck that trend and tally a fourth-quarter loss for the first time since 2018. Many noted similarities between now and eight years ago - not just in the market action, but in what's driving it.

"The prevailing narrative right now is we are repeating the mistakes of 2018," said Brent Donnelly, president of Spectra Markets. He listed three similarities between what was moving markets then and what's driving them now.

Back then, the selloff ended in dramatic fashion, with stocks bottoming on Christmas Eve as then-Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin announced he had held a call with the leaders of the country's largest banks to confirm that they weren't seeing any trouble in the financial system. Ultimately, a cooling in trade tensions with China, and the Federal Reserve's decision to abandon further interest-rate hikes, helped spark a turnaround.
Of course, there's one major difference between now and then: the artificial-intelligence boom.

"Wall Street seems to be at the mercy of tech investors who think Jensen's infidelity and Anthropic's blockbuster market debut may be signs of a top," wrote Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp, in commentary shared with MarketWatch.
-Joseph Adinolfi
